5.34

H. Dative Case: Verbs / Indirect Objects


H.1

Dative Verbs

In Interaktion 5.33 you came across a sentence that reads Und ich helfe dir.

Why dir instead of dich, since it's the object of helfen? In German, a small number of verbs, including the core vocabulary verbs antworten, glauben and helfen, take dative rather than accusative objects.


Warum antwortest du dem Mann nicht?

Why don’t you answer the man?

Glaubst du mir oder ihr?

Do you believe me or her?

Wir helfen diesen Leuten.

We’re helping these people.

Other verbs, such as gefallen and gehören, also appear in most contexts with dative objects, similar to the way their English equivalents use to …


Postmoderne Architektur gefällt diesen Leuten nicht.

These people don’t like postmodernist architecture. (lit.: … doesn’t appeal to these people.)

Das Geld gehört mir, nicht dir.

The money belongs to me, not to you.

You’ll find speakers and writers using gehören + zu, but this doesn't mean to belong to. For example, Er gehört zu mir does not mean He belongs to me (in the sense of ownership) but rather He belongs with me or He is with me. (An extrapolation of this is a sentence such as Wien gehört zu den schönsten Städten der Welt, which means Vienna is counted among the most beautiful cities in the world, or simply Vienna is one of ....) All that to say: To express the literal meaning of X belongs to Y, you should use gehören with a dative object—X gehört Y—rather than gehören + zu.

content:
H.2 Dative: indirect objects


H.2.1

To English speakers, the use of the dative case with a verb such as helfen makes sense if one thinks of helfen as giving help (Hilfe geben). In this phrase, help / Hilfe is a direct object (i.e., what you’re giving), and the person or entity receiving it is the indirect object (i.e., the recipient). In English, indirect objects are expressed in one of two ways:

She’s giving food to the children.

She’s giving the children food.

German prefers the latter construction — using the position of the noun rather than to / zu — and places indirect object nouns and pronouns before direct object nouns:

Sie gibt den Kindern Essen.

Sie gibt ihnen Essen.

Ü5.26
label: Ü5.26

content:
H.2.2

Certain verbs frequently appear with indirect objects:

  • Verbs like geben that denote giving or sharing. These verbs require three sentence elements: Someone who’s doing the giving (the subject: nominative); the object being given (accusative); and the recipient of the object (dative). Notice the relative position of the direct objects and indirect objects in these examples:

    Ich gebe dir 10 Euro. I’ll give you 10 euros. / I’ll give 10 Euros to you.
    Der Professor hat der Gruppe eine sehr schwere Aufgabe gegeben. The professor gave the group a very difficult assignment.

    Either the direct object or the indirect object can be the focus of a question, and that element serves as the question word:

    Was gibst du mir dafür? What will you give me for it?
    Wem gibst du das Geld?

    Who are you giving the money to? / To whom are you giving the money?

  • Erklären usually involves these three elements as well, though it's possible to use it with just a direct object:

    Der Professor erklärt den Studenten die Aufgabe. The professor is explaining the assignment to the students.
    Sie hat mir die Situation erklärt. She explained the situation to me.
    Das erklärt alles! That explains everything!

  • Sagen is used very frequently with the dative case, in the sense of saying something to someone, or telling someone something :

    Er sagt mir nie, was er denkt. He never tells me what he’s thinking.
    Hast du deinen Eltern alles gesagt? Have you told your parents everything? / Did you tell your parents everything?

    You can use sagen without specifying to whom something is being said, that is, with no indirect object in the dative case, in which case it means to say rather than to tell :

    Er sagt nie, was er denkt. He never says what he’s thinking.
    Hast du alles gesagt? Did you say everything? / Have you said everything?

content:
I. Dative: Adjective Endings


I.1

You may still be reeling from learning the adjective endings for the nominative and accusative cases, strong and weak, and you’re wondering what new horror awaits you regarding adjective endings for the dative case. Ready? Here it is:


Adjectives following any article in the dative case take the ending -en.



That’s it.

Here are some samples from the Interaktionen you’ve read in this chapter, with the dative phrases underlined and the endings highlighted:

Das war der Prototyp von der ersten Autobahn.

Hast du die Prüfung beim ersten Mal bestanden?

Hier sehen Sie eine Karte mit den wichtigsten Autobahnen.

We could provide a chart to show this for all three genders and plural nouns, using all the der-words and ein-words, but every single adjective in it would have the same ending: -en.

Ü5.29
label: Ü5.29

content:
I.2

When there's no der- or ein- word in the noun phrase, things are admittedly not quite so simple, but here too the adjective endings are very consistent. As with the nominative and accusative cases, when a dative noun has no preceding article, the adjective ending itself approximates the dative article:


masculine feminine neuter plural
dem→ -em der→ -er dem→ -em den→ -en

This is how these endings appear in actual phrases:


masculine feminine neuter plural
bei starkem Wind mit neuer Technik bei schwachem Licht von schnellen Autos

Phrases with unpreceded adjectives often include plural nouns, and since the adjective ending for these (-en) is identical to the ending used after dative der- and ein- words, it’s easy to remember.
